topic: Impressionism began in Paris in the 1860s–70s: painters such as Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Sisley, Degas and Morisot painted modern life and landscape with visible brushstrokes and bright, unmixed colour.
They worked outdoors (en plein air) to catch passing light and atmosphere, rather than finishing smooth, historical scenes in the studio.
Rejected by the official Salon, they held their own exhibitions from 1874; a critic mocked Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' and gave the group its name.
Impressionism opened the way to modern art: Post-Impressionists (Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin, Seurat) and later Fauvism and Cubism built on it.

Overview: The Impressionists broke academic rules: they painted everyday subjects, outdoors, with free brushwork and pure colour.
Earlier painters, notably Delacroix, Turner and Constable, had already loosened brushwork and paid attention to light and colour.
The movement led directly to Neo-Impressionism, Fauvism and Cubism.
The Impressionism art movement: Under Napoleon III, Haussmann rebuilt Paris and the official Salon decided which artists succeeded; Courbet's Realism had already challenged its taste.
Monet, Renoir, Sisley and Bazille met as students; Manet's 'Olympia' (1863) and 'Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe' scandalised the Salon and made him their hero.
In 1874 the group held the first independent exhibition; Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' (1872) gave them their name. Eight exhibitions followed, the last in 1886.
Their work (Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Degas, Cézanne, Morisot, Cassatt, Caillebotte) slowly won buyers, helped by the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel.
20th-century presentation of Impressioni: In the early 20th century critics argued over how Impressionism should be presented and valued.
Historians such as René Huyghe framed it as the starting point of modern art.
Impressionist techniques: Short, thick strokes of unmixed colour placed side by side, so that colours mix in the viewer's eye.
Painting wet paint into wet paint, outdoors, often finishing a picture in one session.
Shadows painted with colour rather than black; ready-mixed paint in tubes made outdoor work practical.
They drew on earlier masters of loose brushwork such as Rubens, Velázquez and Corot.
Content and composition: Subjects were modern life: cafés, boulevards, railways, leisure, landscapes and ordinary people.
Off-centre, cropped compositions reflect photography and Japanese prints.
Genre painting of everyday life had precedents in the Dutch Golden Age (Jan Steen, Vermeer).
Female Impressionists: Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt, Marie Bracquemond and Eva Gonzalès were central to the movement.
Restricted in where they could go, they often painted domestic and family life, as in Cassatt's 'Afternoon Tea'.
Prominent Impressionists: The central figures were Bazille, Caillebotte, Cassatt, Cézanne, Degas, Guillaumin, Manet, Monet, Morisot, Pissarro, Renoir and Sisley.
Associates and influenced artists: Artists close to the group included Whistler, Jean Béraud and Walter Sickert.
Beyond France: Impressionism spread across Europe and America: Liebermann and Corinth in Germany, Sorolla in Spain, Breitner in the Netherlands, Childe Hassam and Lilla Cabot Perry in the US.
Impressionism in other media: Degas and Rodin brought an Impressionist sense of movement into sculpture.
In music, Debussy and Ravel are often called Impressionists; French film-makers of the 1920s (Gance, Dulac, Epstein) formed an 'Impressionist' cinema.
Post-Impressionism: From the 1880s Seurat (pointillism), Cézanne, Van Gogh and Gauguin kept Impressionism's colour but sought structure, symbolism or emotion.
Works such as 'A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte' and 'The Night Café' led toward 20th-century modern art.
